issues.legal_issue: The authority reviewing a proposed alienation of public trust property must independently assess whether alienation is necessary and whether its terms best serve the trust, and may invite public offers or impose conditions to protect the trust and its beneficiaries.
material_facts: Trustees sought prior sanction for a transaction involving the trust’s immovable property.
The proposed arrangement included development and a sale option, as well as a long-term lease of the land.
issues.conclusion: The Charity Commissioner’s role was not confined to approving or rejecting the trustees’ chosen proposal; the Commissioner had to protect the trust’s interests and could seek competing offers and require the best transaction for the trust.
issues.legal_principle: Section 36(1) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 requires regard to the interest, benefit, and protection of the trust when sanctioning or authorizing alienation. The Charity Commissioner must be objectively satisfied that alienation is necessary and beneficial, and may impose conditions, invite offers, or direct a sale to the person whose proposal is best for the trust. The Court relied on Chenchu Rami Reddy v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, R. Venugopala Naidu v. Venkatarayulu Naidu Charities, Bhaskar Laxman Jadhav v. Karamveer Kakasaheb Wagh Education Society, Mehrwan Homi Irani v. Charity Commissioner, and the Full Bench decision in Sailesh Developers v. Joint Charity Commissioner. The best proposal need not invariably be the one with the highest price; the trust’s interests govern.

predicates.trust_property_alienation_application: Trustees apply for authorization to alienate immovable property held for a public trust.

issues.definition: When trustees seek authorization to alienate public trust property, the authority must assess the need for alienation and ensure that the transaction best serves the trust.

issues.legal_issue: A trust-property transaction cannot be sanctioned when a development arrangement disguises a sale, the transaction is privately negotiated without public notice or reliable assessment of market value, and no exceptional reason justifies that method.
material_facts: The trustees negotiated with a developer before passing the resolution concerning the transaction and invited no competing offers.
The arrangement was described as a development venture but included a sale option that was exercised, and the long-term lease transferred the practical benefit of the land.
No public notice was issued and no reliable process was used to establish the property’s market value.
The application sought to dispense with public notice on the representation that the arrangement was a joint development, although a sale was contemplated and ultimately occurred.
The property was valuable, no development had taken place, and no exceptional circumstance or urgency justified the private transaction.
The Charity Commissioner did not adequately examine whether alienation was necessary or whether the terms protected the trust.
issues.conclusion: The sanction was illegal and was set aside because the transaction did not protect the trust’s interests and had been obtained through a misleading presentation of its nature.
issues.legal_principle: Section 36(1) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 requires the Charity Commissioner to consider the trust’s interest, benefit, and protection; Section 36(2) permits revocation where sanction was obtained by fraud, misrepresentation, or concealment of material facts. Trust property should ordinarily be disposed of through a transparent process that establishes its market value; private negotiation requires special justification. The Court relied on Chenchu Ram Reddy, R. Venugopala Naidu, Bhaskar Laxman Jadhav, Mehrwan Homi Irani, and Sailesh Developers. It distinguished Vedica Procon Private Limited v. Balleshwar Greens Private Limited because the sale there had been confirmed at an adequate price without allegations of fraud, irregularity, or inadequacy, whereas the transaction here had not been supported by a proper market-value assessment and involved material misrepresentation.

rule.if: trust_property_sale_sanction_challenge and sale_option_in_development_deal and nominal_long_term_lease and no_public_notice and no_reliable_market_valuation and application_misrepresented_transaction and not exceptional_reason_for_private_sale

predicates.trust_property_sale_sanction_challenge: A proceeding challenges prior authorization for a transaction that disposes of public trust property.
predicates.sale_option_in_development_deal: The purported development arrangement gives the developer an option to acquire the trust property by sale.
predicates.nominal_long_term_lease: The transaction grants a lease so extensive or nominally priced that it effectively transfers the practical benefit of the property.
predicates.no_public_notice: The trustees proceed without giving public notice or inviting competing offers.
predicates.no_reliable_market_valuation: The trustees and sanctioning authority do not reliably establish the property’s market value.
predicates.application_misrepresented_transaction: The trustees describe the transaction in their application in a way that conceals or misstates its intended sale character.
predicates.exceptional_reason_for_private_sale: A special circumstance or urgent need justifies disposing of the trust property through private negotiation.

issues.definition: If a challenged trust-property transaction combines a disguised sale and an effectively transferring lease with no public notice or reliable market assessment, and the application misstates the transaction without an exceptional reason for private negotiation, the sanction is invalid and must be set aside.

issues.legal_issue: Delay does not bar a challenge to an unlawful sanction for alienating valuable public trust property when development has not begun.
material_facts: The High Court dismissed the challenge mainly because it was brought after the transaction had been known for some time.
Municipal approval for the development had not been granted and no development had taken place.
The transaction concerned valuable public trust property.
issues.conclusion: The delay was not fatal in the circumstances, and the High Court erred in relying on it to dismiss the challenge.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that delay was not decisive on these facts because the proposed development had not occurred and valuable public trust property was at stake. The Court relied on the trust-protection principles in Section 36 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 and the authorities concerning protection of trust property, including Chenchu Ram Reddy and Bhaskar Laxman Jadhav.

predicates.challenge_to_trust_property_sanction: A proceeding challenges a sanction authorizing alienation of public trust property.
predicates.development_not_started: The authorized development has not begun.
predicates.valuable_public_trust_property: The challenged transaction concerns property of substantial value held for a public trust.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns authorization to alienate valuable public trust property and the development has not begun, delay does not bar review.
